title: When Green Does Not Mean Good Growth
author: Whitney Whealdon
summary: Whitney Whealdon uses her weed-ridden autumn lawn as an extended metaphor for standards-based comprehension instruction. Weeds fill the gaps where grass is struggling and make a lawn look healthier than it is, and in the same way data-driven reteaching of discrete standards, gamified apps and a fixation on answer-getting create visible artifacts without building real comprehension. She argues that Sold a Story rightly demanded explicit, systematic teaching of foundational decoding, but that comprehension is a different thing: it is closer to thinking than to a set of skills, and depends on the reader's knowledge, identity, context, the text and the task. Standards are therefore a poor organizing frame for comprehension, and 30 years of teach, assess and reteach has crowded out sustained work with complex texts, talk, writing and knowledge-building. The remedy is to improve the soil, which means practices that are harder to measure and slower to pay off.
points: Practices that look like comprehension support, such as skill-by-skill reteaching, gamified apps and answer-getting, are the "weeds" that mask an unhealthy system rather than fix it.
Foundational reading skills are a constrained set best taught explicitly and systematically, whereas comprehension is dynamic and closer to thinking, so the same approach does not transfer.
Comprehension depends on the interaction of the reader, the text and the task, which is why even strong readers struggle with complex texts in unfamiliar knowledge domains.
Standards-based instruction has crowded out what actually grows comprehension: sustained grappling with complex texts, talking and writing about ideas, and building knowledge.
The long-run cost is less curiosity, stamina and interest in reading, and the fix requires slower, harder-to-measure work rather than quick measurable gains.
quotes: Weeds will take root when the growing conditions are unhealthy, and they can accelerate the decline of healthy growth. They can also disguise the underlying problems for a while.

But like the plush green lawn I thought I saw over the summer that was largely made up of weeds, our comprehension instruction that appears to be doing the job is simply not. Looking green and being healthy are not the same thing.

Foundational reading skills address a constrained set of knowledge and processes that students need to learn to be able to then perform them automatically. Comprehension is different. It is closer to thinking than to a set of discrete skills.

Standards are a poor organizing framework for developing deep comprehension. Even though there are components that can enable comprehension (e.g., fluency, vocabulary, syntax, anaphora, inferential reasoning), we can’t break down a reader’s understanding into discrete skills, teach those skills explicitly, and practice them until students can reliably produce correct answers.

We’ve been led to believe for 30+ years that if we teach and assess standards and then reteach based on weaknesses aligned to standards that kids will get better at comprehension. This is simply not true.
Over time, this can result in less intellectual curiosity, less stamina to stay with something that is difficult before it becomes clear, and less interest in reading overall.

That work will require us to engage in practices that are harder to measure and don’t typically produce immediate gains. Instead of settling for weeds that look like a green lawn, we actually have to grow grass.
